entity.name: Louis Pasteur
entity.description: The French chemist who proved germ theory, invented pasteurization, and developed the first vaccines for rabies and anthrax. Arguably saved more human lives than any other person in history.

story.name: Louis Pasteur
story.description: Discovers molecular chirality with a pair of tweezers, disproves spontaneous generation, invents pasteurization to save the French wine industry, and founds the institute that bears his name. The scientist who proved germs cause disease.

moments.name: Louis Pasteur Is Born to a Tanner's Family in Dole, France
moments.subtitle: A dyslexic boy more interested in fishing and sketching than schoolwork
moments.description: On December 27, 1822, Louis Pasteur was born in Dole, Jura, France, the third child of Jean-Joseph Pasteur, a poor tanner, and Jeanne-Etiennette Roqui. The family moved to Arbois in 1827, where Pasteur attended primary school. He was dyslexic and dysgraphic, and an average student more interested in fishing and drawing pastels than academics. He failed his first university examination in 1841 and earned a mediocre grade in chemistry in 1842. This unremarkable beginning makes his later transformation into one of history's most consequential scientists all the more striking.

moments.name: Pasteur Separates Mirror-Image Crystals with Tweezers and Discovers Molecular Chirality
moments.subtitle: A 25-year-old chemist solves a puzzle that baffled his field by sorting tiny crystals by hand
moments.description: In 1848, 25-year-old Louis Pasteur resolved a longstanding puzzle in chemistry at the Ecole Normale Superieure in Paris. Tartaric acid from living sources rotated polarized light, but synthetic tartaric acid did not, despite having identical chemical composition. Pasteur noticed that crystals of the synthetic compound came in two mirror-image forms. Using tweezers under a microscope, he painstakingly separated the left-handed and right-handed crystals into two piles. Each pile rotated light — but in opposite directions. This was the first demonstration of molecular chirality, a discovery that transformed structural chemistry and later proved essential to pharmacology.

moments.name: Pasteur Disproves Spontaneous Generation with Swan-Neck Flask Experiments
moments.subtitle: Sealed broth stays sterile while open broth breeds life, ending a centuries-old debate
moments.description: In 1859, the French Academy of Sciences challenged scientists to definitively prove or disprove spontaneous generation — the ancient belief that life could arise from nonliving matter. Louis Pasteur designed elegant swan-neck flask experiments: he boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks that allowed air in but trapped dust and microbes. The broth in sealed flasks remained sterile indefinitely, while broth in open flasks quickly teemed with microorganisms. In 1862, the Academy awarded Pasteur the Alhumbert Prize of 2,500 francs. The experiments established that all life comes from existing life, laying the groundwork for germ theory.
moments.address: Ecole Normale Superieure, Rue d'Ulm, Paris, France

moments.name: Pasteur Patents a Heating Process to Save French Wine and Invents Pasteurization
moments.subtitle: A technique designed to cure 'sick' wine ends up saving millions of lives through safe milk
moments.description: In 1865, Louis Pasteur patented a process for heating wine to between 60 and 100 degrees Celsius to kill the bacteria responsible for spoilage — a method that became known as pasteurization. Pasteur had demonstrated by 1862 that microorganisms, not chemical decomposition, caused beverages to spoil. He and Claude Bernard completed key tests on blood and urine on April 20, 1862. The technique was soon applied to beer and, most consequentially, to milk, where it dramatically reduced infant mortality and the spread of diseases like typhoid and tuberculosis. Pasteurization remains a cornerstone of food safety worldwide.

moments.name: Pasteur Founds the Pasteur Institute in Paris and Leads It Until His Death
moments.subtitle: His body is interred in a vault beneath the building, where it remains today
moments.description: In 1887, Louis Pasteur established the Pasteur Institute in Paris, funded largely by an international public subscription following his successful rabies vaccine trials. The institute was inaugurated on November 14, 1888, and Pasteur served as its director until his death on September 28, 1895. Pasteur suffered a severe stroke in 1868 that partially paralyzed his left side, yet he continued working for another 27 years. His body was interred in a neo-Byzantine crypt beneath the institute. The Pasteur Institute grew into one of the world's leading biomedical research centers, with a network that has produced ten Nobel Prize laureates.
moments.address: 25-28 Rue du Docteur Roux, Paris, France
